title: Swiss Embodied AI Unveils Air Humanoid, Hits 98% Reliability
summary: Embodied AI launches Air, a wheeled humanoid with tendon-driven arms that learns factory tasks from workers. Achieves 98% on cable-handling evaluation.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Embodied AI unveiled Air humanoid at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich after nine months of development.
- Air uses tendon-driven arms that yield on contact and learns factory tasks through human demonstration in one month.
- Air achieved 98% reliability on cable-handling evaluation where four competing startups failed to meet 90% target.


Swiss robotics startup[Embodied AI](https://emergent.sh/glossary/embodied-ai) has officially launched Air, a wheeled[humanoid robot](https://emergent.sh/glossary/humanoid-robot) that learns factory tasks through human demonstration and achieved 98% reliability in cable-handling trials. The company unveiled Air on November 6, 2026, at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich, nine months after beginning development, with contracts already signed with major manufacturers globally.


## Tendon-Driven Arms Designed for Safe Human Collaboration


Air uses a lightweight, tendon-driven arm system that distinguishes it from traditional industrial robots. Motors, gearboxes, and electronics are housed in the robot's torso, with tendons controlling the arms. This design allows the arms to yield when they encounter obstructions or make contact with people, reducing injury risk. The company developed Air under ISO/TS 15066:2016, the technical specification addressing collaborative industrial robot safety, with CE marking planned for 2027.


Unlike bipedal humanoid robots, Air moves on wheels for greater stability on flat factory floors. The design prioritizes safety and reliability in physical environments where errors can cause damage or injuries, according to CEO Francesco Stella.


## Human Demonstration Learning With One-Month Transition


Air initially performs jobs under human control, recording activities so Embodied AI's software can learn the movements and eventually perform them independently. The transition from human control to autonomous operation typically takes about one month, depending on task complexity. Human operators remain available to handle unfamiliar situations, while skills learned by one robot can be transferred to others across the fleet.


The company's AI software is already deployed in paid factory installations involving a separate two-armed industrial robot system, providing operational validation ahead of Air's launch.


## 98% Reliability in Cable-Handling Evaluation


In an evaluation conducted by a major consumer electronics manufacturer, Embodied AI achieved 98% reliability on a cable-handling task, exceeding the customer's 90% target. Four other startups participating in the evaluation failed to meet the manufacturer's requirements. The cable-handling test represents a challenging use case for robotics: precise hand movements in repetitive tasks that frequently change, making them difficult to automate with conventional systems.


## Release Date and Production Plans


Air was officially launched on November 6, 2026, at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich. Embodied AI is preparing for larger-scale production after signing contracts with major manufacturers globally. The company is backed by Faber, which led its first funding round, along with TechShop, Look AI Ventures, Plug and Play, and Vento.


## EPFL Research Roots and Team Background


Air's tendon-driven arm design grew out of CEO Francesco Stella's doctoral research at EPFL, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. Stella previously conducted research at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He co-founded Embodied AI with CTO Kai Junge and COO Max Polzin, both of whom hold doctoral backgrounds in robotics.


## What This Means


Embodied AI's Air launch represents a practical step toward safe human-robot collaboration in manufacturing environments where traditional automation has struggled. The 98% reliability benchmark on cable-handling tasks, combined with the one-month learning transition and safety-focused tendon-driven design, positions Air as a viable solution for manufacturers seeking to automate repetitive manual work without replacing human expertise entirely. The wheeled form factor and ISO safety compliance signal a focus on near-term deployment over the more speculative bipedal humanoid approaches pursued by other robotics startups.
